chapter.title: How should I act: Mill against Kant

cards.body: A murderer knocks on your door and asks where your friend is hiding, and Kant, writing in 1797, said you still may not lie. At the long dinner table, this is where the plates start to rattle. Kant asks of any act *could everyone do this?*, while Mill, a guest who arrives decades later, asks **does it make the most happiness?**
cards.simpler: Imagine a murderer knocks on your door and asks where your friend is hiding. Kant, writing in 1797, said you still may not lie. At the long dinner table, this is where the plates start to rattle. Kant asks of any act, *could everyone do this?* Mill, a guest who arrives decades later, asks something else: **does it make the most happiness?**

cards.prompt: Your friend Priya made you promise to help her move flat on Saturday. At 9am on Saturday, your neighbour's kid needs a lift to hospital. Which guest at the table would start by counting who ends up better off?

options.text: Neither. They'd both just say keep your word.

whyNot.a: That's Kant's test, not Mill's: Kant asks whether the rule could work for everyone, not who ends up happier.
whyNot.c: That assumes they agree, but they ask different questions: only Mill's question is about counting results.

cards.reteach: Two guests, two questions. Mill looks at outcomes: who gets hurt, who gets helped, add it up. Kant looks at the rule behind your choice and asks if everyone could follow it.

cards.title: Mill's test: weigh the results
cards.body:
John Stuart Mill set out his test in an 1861 book called *Utilitarianism* (from *utility*, an old word for usefulness). An action is right if it **produces the most happiness and the least suffering** for everyone it touches. You count as one person. So does a stranger.

Picture a kitchen scale on the dinner table. Pile the good results on one side and the pain on the other, then watch which way it tips.

You'd think right and wrong live inside the act itself. For Mill, the act is just a lever. What counts is what it moves.
cards.simpler: In 1861, John Stuart Mill wrote a book called *Utilitarianism*, from *utility*, an old word for usefulness. An action is right, he said, if it **makes the most happiness and the least suffering** for everyone it touches. You count as one person, and so does a stranger. Picture a kitchen scale: good results on one side, pain on the other. Which way does it tip? For Mill, the act matters only for what it leads to.

cards.title: Mill at the door, and at Aunt Rosa's
cards.body: Run the murderer through Mill's scale. If you lie, your friend lives and the murderer wastes an evening. If you tell the truth, your friend probably dies. The scale slams down: **Mill's test says lie.** Now smaller stakes: Aunt Rosa hands you a mustard-yellow jumper she spent three months knitting and asks if you love it. A quick tally of results says yes, warmly, and wear it to lunch. Mill himself was warier: he thought even small, handy lies wear down the trust that makes anyone's word worth believing.
cards.simpler: Put the murderer on Mill's scale. If you lie, your friend lives and the murderer wastes an evening. If you tell the truth, your friend probably dies. The scale drops hard on one side: **Mill's test says lie.** Now try something smaller. Aunt Rosa hands you a mustard-yellow jumper she spent three months knitting and asks if you love it. A quick count of results says yes, say it warmly, and wear it to lunch. But Mill himself was more careful: he thought even small lies slowly wear down how much people trust each other's words.

cards.prompt: Sam promised to meet Jo for coffee at 3pm. At 2:50 a stranger's car is stuck in the mud, and helping would make Sam 20 minutes late. Using only Mill's test, what should Sam ask?

options.text: Which choice leaves the most people better off, counting Jo's annoyance too?
Could everyone break small promises whenever it suited them?
I promised, so does anything else even matter?

whyNot.b: That's Kant's question, not Mill's: it tests the rule, not the results.
whyNot.c: That's treating the promise as fixed no matter what, not Mill's scale: Mill weighs the promise like any other result, including Jo waiting alone.

cards.reteach: Mill doesn't ignore promises. He puts them on the scale. Jo's 20 lonely minutes go on one side, the stranger's stuck car on the other, and the heavier side decides.

cards.title: Kant's test: could the rule survive?
cards.body:
Immanuel Kant, writing in 1785, ignored the scale. Before you act, he said, turn your reason into a rule for everyone, such as *anyone may lie when it helps them*. If that rule **would break itself once everyone followed it**, the act is wrong.

Lying fails this test. A lie works like a fake banknote: it only buys anything while most notes are real. If everyone lied whenever it was handy, nobody would believe anyone, and lying would stop working.

So the two tests split. At the murderer's knock, Mill lies and Kant won't. On Aunt Rosa's jumper, Kant still says no, while a quick tally says yes and Mill himself might hesitate. On keeping an ordinary promise, they usually agree, but for different reasons.
cards.simpler: Immanuel Kant, writing in 1785, ignored the scale. Turn your reason into a rule for everyone, such as *anyone may lie when it helps them*. If that rule **would break itself once everyone followed it**, the act is wrong. Lying fails. Like a fake banknote, a lie only works while most notes are real. If everyone lied, nobody would believe anyone. At the murderer's door, Mill lies and Kant won't. Over Aunt Rosa's jumper, Kant still won't, and even Mill might pause.

cards.body: Dev explains Kant to a friend: if everyone cheated on taxes, the roads would crumble, so cheating is wrong. It sounds like Kant, but it's really **Mill in a Kant costume**, because Dev is counting bad results. Mill made this same jab at Kant in 1861, arguing that Kant's test only ever showed the results would be bad. The tell: if the answer is about what *happens*, it's Mill; Kant asks whether the rule *undoes itself*.
cards.simpler: Dev tells a friend about Kant: if everyone cheated on taxes, the roads would fall apart, so cheating is wrong. It sounds like Kant, but it's really **Mill in a Kant costume**, because Dev is counting bad results. Mill made this same point against Kant in 1861, saying Kant's test only ever showed the results would be bad. Here's the clue: if the answer is about what *happens*, it's Mill. Kant asks whether the rule *undoes itself*.

cards.prompt: Lena lent you her bike and you promised it back by Friday. Three friends explain why you should return it. Which one is running Kant's test?

options.text: Lena will be happier with her bike than I'd be keeping it.
If everyone broke promises when it was handy, nobody would trust a promise, so mine would mean nothing.
If everyone broke promises, the world would be a more miserable place.

whyNot.a: That's Mill's scale, not Kant's rule test: it weighs Lena's happiness against yours.
whyNot.c: That's Mill in a Kant costume: it starts with 'if everyone' but then counts misery, which is a result.

cards.reteach: Kant's test isn't about how bad things would get. It asks whether the rule would cancel itself out: a promise only means something while people keep them. If the reason talks about misery or happiness, it's Mill's.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Mill judges an action by its results: **whatever makes the most happiness wins**, so at the murderer's door, he lies. Kant judges the rule behind it: if the rule would collapse once everyone followed it, don't do it, not at the door and not over Aunt Rosa's jumper.
cards.simpler: Mill judges an action by what it leads to: **whatever makes the most happiness wins**, so at the murderer's door, he tells the lie. Kant judges the rule behind the action. If that rule would fall apart once everyone followed it, don't do it, not to the murderer at your door and not about Aunt Rosa's jumper.

cards.body:
Pick one small choice you made today: a white lie, a skipped reply, a borrowed charger. Ask Mill's question (what did it lead to?) and Kant's (could everyone do it?). Notice whether they agree.

Tomorrow: why 'God is dead' was meant as a warning, not a boast.
cards.simpler: Pick one small choice you made today, like a white lie, a reply you skipped, or a charger you borrowed. First ask Mill's question: what did it lead to? Then ask Kant's question: could everyone do it? Then **notice whether the two answers agree**, and think about why they might not. Tomorrow: why 'God is dead' was meant as a warning, not a boast.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now run a dilemma through Mill's test and Kant's test and say where they give different answers.

dubious_claims: Aunt Rosa example: 'Mill's test says yes, warmly' presents the white lie as Mill's verdict, but in Utilitarianism (1861, ch. 2) Mill warns against 'expedient' lies because they weaken trust in what people say; he allows only narrow exceptions, like hiding facts from a wrongdoer. A simple add-up-the-results reading supports the line. Mill himself likely would not.
Kant card: 'On Aunt Rosa's jumper, the same split' depends on that same disputed reading of Mill.
repairedFrom.why: The 'In one breath' card is a bare summary with almost no image, and it holds the 'Tomorrow' teaser, so the chapter's real last line is the try card, not the hook into the next chapter.
repairedFrom.fix: Move 'Tomorrow: why "God is dead" was meant as a warning, not a boast.' to the end of the try card, and put the door and the jumper back into the summary (e.g. 'Mill lies at the door and praises the jumper; Kant does neither').
